prompt.context: Our client is a cell phone operator in the Midwest of the United States. The CEO has hired Bain & Company to advise him on strategy for the next five years. You are one of the consultants on this project and are responsible for the sales effectiveness strategy. The company currently has three direct sales channels: owned retail stores, in-bound (responsive) call center, and an outbound (proactive) call center.
prompt.question: Based on the economics of each channel, what do you advise the CEO to focus on in terms of the most effective and profitable sales channels?

clarifying_info.q: Do we have data on customer segmentation within each channel?
clarifying_info.a: No, the client does not have insight about customer segmentation in each of the channels.

clarifying_info.q: What is the traffic volume for each channel?
clarifying_info.a: In-bound call center: 10 million customers (note: the interviewee later corrects this to 20 million to account for the 50/50 split). Out-bound call center: 1 million customers. Retail stores: 1 million customers.

clarifying_info.q: Does any of the in-bound call center traffic represent customer service rather than sales?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. The in-bound call center also serves as a customer service channel in a 50/50 split (sales vs. customer service). Every customer visiting a retail store generates revenue, and the out-bound call center focuses only on sales.

clarifying_info.q: What is the success rate (conversion rate) per channel?
clarifying_info.a: In-bound call center: 10%. Out-bound call center: 50%. Retail stores: 50%.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average revenue per customer per channel?
clarifying_info.a: In-bound call center: $40. Out-bound call center: $50. Retail stores: $85.

clarifying_info.q: What is the total cost per channel?
clarifying_info.a: In-bound call center: $1 million. Out-bound call center: $1 million. Retail stores: $10 million.

clarifying_info.q: What is the fixed vs. variable cost split per channel?
clarifying_info.a: In-bound call center: 50% fixed / 50% variable. Out-bound call center: 25% fixed / 75% variable. Retail stores: 80% fixed / 20% variable.

clarifying_info.q: Do we know the churn rate per channel to calculate Customer Lifetime Value?
clarifying_info.a: No, but the client believes churn is the same across all segments.

exhibits.title: Channel Key Facts Table
exhibits.shows: A table summarizing key metrics for each of the three sales channels: in-bound call center, out-bound call center, and owned retail stores. Rows include success rate, traffic, average revenue, fixed/variable cost split, total cost, and customer service time proportion.

framework: Understand the three channels and their purpose (sales vs. customer service)
Calculate sales-relevant traffic per channel (adjusting in-bound for 50% customer service share)
Calculate total revenues per channel: sales traffic x success rate x average revenue
Calculate revenue per new customer acquired per channel
Decompose costs into fixed and variable components
Calculate variable cost per unit of relevant traffic
Compare contribution margin across channels (revenue per new customer minus variable cost per relevant traffic)
Assess scalability risk: channels with high variable cost ratios are more expensive to grow
Synthesize: recommend the channel with the best variable economics and growth potential

questions.prompt: Calculate total revenues for each channel.
questions.guidance: Candidate must recognize that in-bound call center traffic of 10M (or 20M in the interviewee's corrected version) is split 50/50 between sales and customer service, so only half generates sales leads. Then apply success rate and average revenue.

math.setup: Revenue = (Sales-relevant traffic) x (Success rate) x (Avg revenue per customer). In-bound: sales-relevant traffic = 20M x 50% = 10M. Out-bound and Retail: full 1M traffic is sales-relevant.

questions.prompt: Calculate revenue per new customer acquired for each channel.
questions.guidance: Divide total channel revenue by the number of new customers acquired (sales-relevant traffic). This normalizes revenue to a per-acquisition basis.

math.setup: Revenue per new customer = Total revenue / (Sales-relevant traffic). New customers acquired = sales-relevant traffic (not converted traffic; see casebook logic where revenue per relevant contact is used).

questions.prompt: Calculate variable costs and variable cost per unit of relevant traffic for each channel.
questions.guidance: Multiply total cost by the variable cost percentage to get total variable costs. Then divide by sales-relevant traffic to get cost per relevant contact. This reveals which channel is cheapest to scale on a marginal basis.

math.setup: Variable cost = Total cost x variable cost %. Variable cost per relevant traffic = Variable cost / Sales-relevant traffic.
steps: In-bound variable cost: $1M x 50% = $500K; per relevant traffic: $500K / (20M x 50%) = $500K / 10M = $0.05
Out-bound variable cost: $1M x 75% = $750K; per relevant traffic: $750K / 1M = $0.75
Retail variable cost: $10M x 20% = $2M; per relevant traffic: $2M / 1M = $2.00

questions.prompt: Compare contribution margins across channels and identify investment risk by fixed cost structure.
questions.guidance: Contribution margin per channel = revenue per new customer minus variable cost per relevant traffic. Separately, note that channels with a high variable cost share (out-bound: 75%) will see total costs rise fastest if volume is scaled, making them riskier investments. Channels with high fixed costs (retail: 80%) have lower marginal cost but high sunk commitments.

math.setup: Contribution margin (approximate) = Revenue per new customer - Variable cost per relevant contact.
steps: In-bound: $4.00 - $0.05 = $3.95 (low revenue but extremely low variable cost)
Fixed cost shares: In-bound 50%, Out-bound 25%, Retail 80% — Out-bound has the highest variable cost share (75%), so scaling it raises total costs most aggressively
math.answer: Retail has the highest absolute contribution margin; In-bound has the lowest variable cost per contact; Out-bound's high variable ratio means its total cost is most sensitive to volume increases.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key strategic considerations when deciding which sales channel(s) to invest in?

categories.name: Revenue drivers
ideas: Revenue per new customer acquired (Retail $42.50 >> Out-bound $25 >> In-bound $4)
Conversion/success rate (Retail and Out-bound 50% vs In-bound 10%)
Total revenue generated at current scale (In-bound $40M, Retail $42.5M, Out-bound $25M)

categories.name: Cost structure
ideas: Variable cost per relevant contact (In-bound $0.05 is by far the lowest)
Total cost to serve (Retail $10M vs $1M each for the call centers)
Fixed vs. variable mix — high fixed cost (Retail 80%) means low marginal cost but high break-even risk; high variable cost (Out-bound 75%) means total cost grows fast with volume

categories.name: Scalability and investment risk
ideas: Channels with high variable costs (Out-bound) become more expensive as you invest — higher risk
Retail stores require large upfront capital (80% fixed) and are hard to downsize
In-bound call center has the lowest marginal cost and is already handling large traffic volumes

categories.name: Channel purpose and traffic quality
ideas: In-bound also serves 50% customer service — dilutes sales effectiveness and may inflate apparent traffic
Out-bound is purely sales-focused and proactively targets customers
Retail captures high-value customers willing to visit a store, explaining the higher revenue per customer

categories.name: Customer lifetime value considerations
ideas: Churn is assumed equal across channels, so CLV differences are driven by initial revenue per acquisition
Higher acquisition revenue (Retail) implies higher CLV even if churn is equal
In-bound's low revenue per new customer may indicate lower-value customer segment or cross-sell untapped potential

recommendation: Focus investment on the in-bound call center, which offers by far the lowest variable cost per relevant contact ($0.05 vs $0.75 and $2.00), giving it the most attractive economics for scaling sales activity.

The client should diagnose why the in-bound channel generates such low revenue per new customer ($4) despite high traffic, and identify opportunities to increase revenue through upselling, cross-selling, or improving the sales-to-customer-service ratio.
Avoid heavy investment in the out-bound call center in the near term: its high variable cost share (75%) means total costs will escalate most quickly if volume is expanded.

Retail stores generate the highest revenue per customer and are valuable, but require $10M in cost (80% fixed) — further expansion requires careful analysis of store-level unit economics before committing additional capital.
risks: In-bound channel's low per-customer revenue ($4) may reflect a structurally different — and lower-value — customer segment that cannot easily be upsold.
Increasing in-bound sales capacity may be constrained by the channel's dual role as a customer service line.
Retail stores may serve as a brand anchor and drive awareness that indirectly benefits other channels — cutting back could have spillover effects.
Out-bound call center churn and regulatory risk (do-not-call lists, compliance) could limit its effectiveness.
next_steps: Conduct root-cause analysis on in-bound channel's low conversion rate (10%) and low average revenue ($40) to determine if improvement is feasible.
Build unit economics model for retail stores at the individual store level to identify high-performing vs. underperforming locations.
Pilot upsell/cross-sell scripts in in-bound call center and measure revenue uplift.
Reassess channel mix once CLV data by channel becomes available (currently assumed equal).
